question.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨2t-{t}^{2}\,,\,2{t}^{2}\,,\,2t+{t}^{2}⟩,$ find the point at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,1⟩.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t+{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2-2t,\,4t,\,2+2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,1⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c\,⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,1⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c\,⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,1⟩ \\ ⟨2-2t,\,4t,\,2+2t⟩ & =c\,⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,1⟩ \\ ⟨2-2t,\,4t,\,2+2t⟩ & =⟨0\,,\,c\,,\,c⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2-2t=0 \\ 4t=c \\ 2+2t=c\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we obtain that $t=1.$ Substituting to the second equation, we get $c=4.$
These values also satisfy the third equation. 

Therefore, $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨2-{1}^{2}\,,\,2\cdot {1}^{2}\,,\,2+{1}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,2,\,3⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(1,2,3).$
